                    ### Question
                    A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because she is concerned he is having another stroke. The patient says he woke up with right-sided facial weakness and drooping. Past medical history is significant for a recent case of shingles treated with acyclovir, and a stroke, diagnosed 10 years ago, from which he recovered with no residual functional deficits. On physical examination, there is weakness and drooping of the entire right side of the face. Sensation is intact. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following additional findings would also most likely be seen in this patient?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Decreased salivation
opb. Partial hearing loss
opc. Complete loss of taste to the tongue
opd. Wrinkled forehead
ope. Expressive aphasia

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's right-sided facial weakness and drooping suggest involvement of the facial nerve (CN VII), commonly associated with Bell's palsy, especially given the recent history of shingles. In Bell's palsy, the entire side of the face is affected, including the forehead, which would not wrinkle, contradicting the option of a 'wrinkled forehead.' Decreased salivation and partial hearing loss can occur due to the facial nerve's role in salivation and its proximity to the auditory structures. Complete loss of taste to the tongue is unlikely, as the facial nerve primarily affects taste in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the entire tongue. Expressive aphasia is unrelated to facial nerve function and is more associated with cortical damage, such as from a stroke affecting Broca's area. Therefore, the most likely additional finding in this patient, consistent with facial nerve involvement, is decreased salivation.
